claims.source_title: AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Role of Biomarkers for the Management of Ulcerative Colitis
claims.claim_text: AGA suggests that for people with ulcerative colitis who are in symptomatic remission (feeling well), a biomarker test, such as a stool test, may help monitoring when it is used together with symptoms rather than relying on symptoms alone. Your clinician decides which tests are right for you.
claims.original_claim_text: In people with ulcerative colitis in symptomatic remission, the AGA guideline panel suggests a monitoring strategy that combines a non-invasive biomarker with symptoms rather than symptoms alone.
claims.supporting_excerpt: In patients with UC in symptomatic remission, the panel suggests the use of a biomarker- and symptom-based monitoring strategy over a symptom-based monitoring strategy.
claims.precise_locator: Abstract (structured), Results section — Europe PMC record EXT_ID:36822736; Gastroenterology 2023;164(3):344-372. Page/statement-level locators require full text (link_only).
claims.limitations: Conditional recommendation; the guideline does not specify monitoring frequency in the retrieved abstract. Applies to established UC, not diagnosis. Wording edited after owner safety review (2026-11-17); 'suggests'/'may' mirror the conditional GRADE recommendation. Not a basis for changing treatment or skipping endoscopy.
claims.applicability_limitations: Adults with established ulcerative colitis | conditional guideline recommendation (GRADE; AGA)
claims.plain_language_explanation: AGA suggests that for people with ulcerative colitis who are in symptomatic remission (feeling well), a biomarker test, such as a stool test, may help monitoring when it is used together with symptoms rather than relying on symptoms alone. Your clinician decides which tests are right for you.

claims.source_title: AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Role of Biomarkers for the Management of Ulcerative Colitis
claims.claim_text: For people with ulcerative colitis in symptomatic remission, AGA suggests that a fecal calprotectin below 150 µg/g, a normal fecal lactoferrin and/or a normal CRP may help rule out active inflammation, so that routine endoscopy may not be needed. 150 µg/g is a guideline decision threshold, not a diagnosis for any one person: results vary between tests and between days. Your clinician interprets them with your symptoms and decides whether an endoscopy is needed; do not skip or delay a scope or a clinic visit because of a test result.
claims.original_claim_text: For a person with ulcerative colitis in symptomatic remission, the panel suggests using fecal calprotectin below 150 micrograms per gram, a normal fecal lactoferrin, and/or a normal CRP to rule out active inflammation and avoid routine endoscopic assessment.
claims.supporting_excerpt: For patients in symptomatic remission, the panel suggests using fecal calprotectin <150 μg/g, normal fecal lactoferrin, and/or normal CRP to rule out active inflammation and avoid routine endoscopic assessment of disease.
claims.precise_locator: Abstract (structured), Results section — Europe PMC record EXT_ID:36822736; Gastroenterology 2023;164(3):344-372. Page/statement-level locators require full text (link_only).
claims.limitations: Conditional recommendation. 150 μg/g is a guideline decision threshold, not a diagnostic cut-off for an individual; calprotectin assays are not interchangeable and vary within-day / within-stool. Wording edited after owner safety review (2026-11-17); 'suggests'/'may' mirror the conditional GRADE recommendation. Not a basis for changing treatment or skipping endoscopy.
claims.applicability_limitations: Adults with established ulcerative colitis | conditional guideline recommendation (GRADE; AGA)
claims.plain_language_explanation: For people with ulcerative colitis in symptomatic remission, AGA suggests that a fecal calprotectin below 150 µg/g, a normal fecal lactoferrin and/or a normal CRP may help rule out active inflammation, so that routine endoscopy may not be needed. 150 µg/g is a guideline decision threshold, not a diagnosis for any one person: results vary between tests and between days. Your clinician interprets them with your symptoms and decides whether an endoscopy is needed; do not skip or delay a scope or a clinic visit because of a test result.

claims.source_title: AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Role of Biomarkers for the Management of Ulcerative Colitis
claims.claim_text: For people with ulcerative colitis who have moderate-to-severe symptoms, AGA suggests that a fecal calprotectin above 150 µg/g, an elevated fecal lactoferrin or an elevated CRP may help a clinician decide on treatment without routine endoscopy. 150 µg/g is a guideline threshold, not a diagnosis for any one person, and any treatment change is decided by your clinician, not by a test result alone.
claims.original_claim_text: For a person with ulcerative colitis who has moderate-to-severe symptoms, the panel suggests using fecal calprotectin above 150 micrograms per gram, an elevated fecal lactoferrin, or an elevated CRP to inform treatment decisions and avoid routine endoscopic assessment.
claims.supporting_excerpt: In patients with UC with moderate to severe symptoms, the panel suggests using fecal calprotectin >150 μg/g, elevated fecal lactoferrin, or elevated CRP to inform treatment decisions and avoid routine endoscopic assessment of disease.
claims.precise_locator: Abstract (structured), Results section — Europe PMC record EXT_ID:36822736; Gastroenterology 2023;164(3):344-372. Page/statement-level locators require full text (link_only).
claims.limitations: Conditional recommendation. Concordant elevated biomarker + moderate/severe symptoms; interpretation and any treatment change are clinician-led. Wording edited after owner safety review (2026-11-17); 'suggests'/'may' mirror the conditional GRADE recommendation. Not a basis for changing treatment or skipping endoscopy.
claims.applicability_limitations: Adults with established ulcerative colitis | conditional guideline recommendation (GRADE; AGA)
claims.plain_language_explanation: For people with ulcerative colitis who have moderate-to-severe symptoms, AGA suggests that a fecal calprotectin above 150 µg/g, an elevated fecal lactoferrin or an elevated CRP may help a clinician decide on treatment without routine endoscopy. 150 µg/g is a guideline threshold, not a diagnosis for any one person, and any treatment change is decided by your clinician, not by a test result alone.

claims.source_title: AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Role of Biomarkers for the Management of Ulcerative Colitis
claims.claim_text: When symptoms and biomarker tests disagree (for example feeling well but with raised markers, or moderate-to-severe symptoms with normal markers), AGA suggests that a clinician may consider an endoscopic assessment before adjusting treatment. Do not change your treatment yourself.
claims.original_claim_text: When symptoms and biomarkers disagree in ulcerative colitis — symptomatic remission with elevated biomarkers, or moderate-to-severe symptoms with normal biomarkers — the panel suggests endoscopic assessment of disease to inform treatment decisions.
claims.supporting_excerpt: However, in patients in symptomatic remission but elevated biomarkers, and in patients with moderate to severe symptoms with normal biomarkers, the panel suggests endoscopic assessment of disease to inform treatment decisions.
claims.precise_locator: Abstract (structured), Results section — Europe PMC record EXT_ID:36822736; Gastroenterology 2023;164(3):344-372. Page/statement-level locators require full text (link_only).
claims.limitations: Conditional recommendation. Explicitly a case where non-invasive biomarkers are insufficient and endoscopy is preferred. Wording edited after owner safety review (2026-11-17); 'suggests'/'may' mirror the conditional GRADE recommendation. Not a basis for changing treatment or skipping endoscopy.
claims.applicability_limitations: Adults with established ulcerative colitis | conditional guideline recommendation (GRADE; AGA)
claims.plain_language_explanation: When symptoms and biomarker tests disagree (for example feeling well but with raised markers, or moderate-to-severe symptoms with normal markers), AGA suggests that a clinician may consider an endoscopic assessment before adjusting treatment. Do not change your treatment yourself.

claims.claim_text: For people with ulcerative colitis who have only mild symptoms, AGA suggests that an endoscopic assessment of disease activity may be used to help a clinician make treatment decisions.
claims.original_claim_text: For a person with ulcerative colitis who has only mild symptoms, the panel suggests endoscopic assessment of disease activity to inform treatment decisions.
claims.supporting_excerpt: In patients with UC with mild symptoms, the panel suggests endoscopic assessment of disease activity to inform treatment decisions.

claims.source_title: AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Role of Biomarkers for the Management of Ulcerative Colitis
claims.claim_text: The AGA guideline panel identified the choice between biomarker-based monitoring and endoscopy-based monitoring as a knowledge gap, so it is not known which approach is better. This means the guideline's biomarker suggestions should not be read as showing that biomarkers are better than endoscopy.
claims.original_claim_text: The AGA guideline panel made 7 conditional recommendations on biomarker use in ulcerative colitis, and identified using a biomarker-based rather than an endoscopy-based monitoring strategy as a knowledge gap.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The panel identified the use of a biomarker-based monitoring strategy over an endoscopy-based monitoring strategy as a knowledge gap.
claims.precise_locator: Abstract (structured), Results section — Europe PMC record EXT_ID:36822736; Gastroenterology 2023;164(3):344-372. Page/statement-level locators require full text (link_only).
claims.limitations: This is a statement about evidence limitations, not a management recommendation. All recommendations in the guideline are conditional. Wording edited after owner safety review (2026-11-17); 'suggests'/'may' mirror the conditional GRADE recommendation. Not a basis for changing treatment or skipping endoscopy.
claims.applicability_limitations: Adults with established ulcerative colitis | guideline-identified knowledge gap
claims.plain_language_explanation: The AGA guideline panel identified the choice between biomarker-based monitoring and endoscopy-based monitoring as a knowledge gap, so it is not known which approach is better. This means the guideline's biomarker suggestions should not be read as showing that biomarkers are better than endoscopy.

claims.source_title: AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Role of Biomarkers for the Management of Ulcerative Colitis
claims.claim_text: The AGA guideline concludes that non-invasive tests - fecal calprotectin, fecal lactoferrin and blood CRP - can inform monitoring and management of ulcerative colitis. Your clinician decides how to use them for you.
claims.original_claim_text: The guideline concludes that in ulcerative colitis, non-invasive biomarkers including fecal calprotectin, fecal lactoferrin and serum CRP can inform disease monitoring and management.
claims.supporting_excerpt: In patients with UC, noninvasive biomarkers, including fecal calprotectin, fecal lactoferrin, and serum CRP can inform disease monitoring and management.
claims.precise_locator: Abstract (structured), Conclusions section — Europe PMC record EXT_ID:36822736; Gastroenterology 2023;164(3):344-372.
claims.limitations: 'Can inform' - supportive, not a mandate to replace clinical or endoscopic assessment. Conditional-recommendation evidence base. Wording edited after owner safety review (2026-11-17); 'suggests'/'may' mirror the conditional GRADE recommendation. Not a basis for changing treatment or skipping endoscopy.
claims.applicability_limitations: Adults with established ulcerative colitis | guideline conclusion (GRADE; AGA)
claims.plain_language_explanation: The AGA guideline concludes that non-invasive tests - fecal calprotectin, fecal lactoferrin and blood CRP - can inform monitoring and management of ulcerative colitis. Your clinician decides how to use them for you.

claims.source_title: A randomized controlled trial of alternate-day versus daily iron therapy in ulcerative colitis in remission
claims.claim_text: In a small randomized, open-label study of 56 people with ulcerative colitis in remission who had iron-deficiency anaemia, the researchers did not detect a statistically significant difference in haemoglobin, red-cell indices or iron measures between daily and alternate-day oral iron after 8 weeks, and adverse events and flares were also not significantly different between the groups. This does not prove that the two schedules are equivalent, and it is not a recommendation to change iron dosing: talk to a clinician before changing how you take iron.
claims.original_claim_text: In a small randomized, open-label study of 56 people with ulcerative colitis in remission who had iron-deficiency anaemia, the researchers did not detect a statistically significant difference in haemoglobin, red-cell indices or iron measures between daily and alternate-day oral iron after 8 weeks, and adverse events and flares were also not significantly different between the groups. This does not prove that the two schedules are equivalent, and it is not a recommendation to change iron dosing: talk to a clinician before changing how you take iron.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Our study did not show any significant difference in mean hemoglobin levels, RBC indices, or iron profiles between the daily and alternate-day oral iron groups. Adverse events and disease flare were also not statistically significant in the two groups.
claims.limitations: 56 participants, open-label, 8 weeks, one oral iron formulation, single country; the authors say larger studies are needed. 'No significant difference' does not prove the two schedules are equivalent.
claims.applicability_limitations: Adults with ulcerative colitis in remission and iron-deficiency anaemia (n = 56) | single small open-label randomized trial (low)
claims.plain_language_explanation: In a small randomized, open-label study of 56 people with ulcerative colitis in remission who had iron-deficiency anaemia, the researchers did not detect a statistically significant difference in haemoglobin, red-cell indices or iron measures between daily and alternate-day oral iron after 8 weeks, and adverse events and flares were also not significantly different between the groups. This does not prove that the two schedules are equivalent, and it is not a recommendation to change iron dosing: talk to a clinician before changing how you take iron.

claims.source_title: European Crohn’s and Colitis Organisation consensus on dietary management of inflammatory bowel disease
claims.claim_text: A European consensus statement (ECCO, 2025) gives low-level, expert-opinion advice (evidence level 5; 100% agreement among panel members) for people with inflammatory bowel disease in general, not just ulcerative colitis: unless an IBD clinician recommends a specific diet, follow the healthy-eating guidelines for the general population. This is general, low-evidence IBD-wide advice, not a UC-specific treatment.
claims.original_claim_text: Statement 1: In the absence of a specific dietary intervention that is recommended by an IBD healthcare professional, healthy eating guidelines should be followed by people with IBD, as recommended for the general population. (EL5) (Consensus: 100%)
claims.supporting_excerpt: Statement 1: In the absence of a specific dietary intervention that is recommended by an IBD healthcare professional, healthy eating guidelines should be followed by people with IBD, as recommended for the general population. (EL5) (Consensus: 100%)
claims.precise_locator: Re-issue of live claim CLM-081 (same verbatim excerpt and source locator)
claims.verification_status: verbatim excerpt carried over from live claim CLM-081
claims.limitations: Low-evidence (EL5) expert consensus for IBD in general; not specific to ulcerative colitis. Re-issue of live claim CLM-081 with clearer labelling (owner decision 2026-11-17); the original is preserved in prototype-v1.
claims.applicability_limitations: IBD-wide statement; UC is covered at source level only

This is general, low-evidence IBD-wide advice, not a UC-specific treatment.

claims.claim_text: A patient-information page from Crohn's & Colitis UK says there is not enough high-quality evidence to know for certain whether drinking alcohol could increase your risk of a flare-up. This is a statement of uncertainty: it does not mean alcohol is safe, and it does not mean it is harmful for you. Talk to your clinician about alcohol.
